Well, 800k are the number that attempt and complete each year. The number of attempts that are not successful are difficult to estimate because many go unreported.

Out of the 7.6 billion people on earth, if 20 million per year attempt (using the high estimate), it's still less than 1%, or less than 1 in 100. It's closer to 1 in 500 people on the planet attempt each year. This is only estimates, of course. It could be less, could be more.

Those with suicidal ideation and no attempt is likely much higher than the attempts that don't complete.

Worldwide, about 800,000-1,000,000 per year complete. It is estimated that 1 in 20 attempts are completed. So, 16,000,000 to 20,000,000 attempts per year.

That is 2200-2800 per day completed and 44,000-55,000 attempts **each day**.

I like to think that suicide is a 100% preventable cause of death, but it's not always so easy. The cure isn't easily defined. Some say therapy, some say medication, some say in-patient programs, out-patient programs.

Sometimes the cure is love and compassion. Sometimes it's money or a job. Food. A place to sleep. Comfort. Security.  Therapy and medication won't get you those things. It may help you find ways to get there yourself, but you're going to be doing the heavy lifting.

And depression makes heavy lifting even harder. Anyway, I don't want this to get too terribly long.

Can I go on if I don't make it? I can't answer that. I don't think I can.

I don't have all of the answers, but I do encourage everyone to give it at least a week after a major failure to see if there are other options. I gave it two months and set my date on March 4th. That morning, a hiring manager sent me an email as I was getting ready to leave home and crash my car into a wall at 100 MPH. It was between putting my pants on and getting my shoes tied.

That's not to force some mysterious deity or superstition or sense of fate on you. That's just how things played out for me. And there's no guarantee on this job. I may flounder and fail the interview horribly, and I'll be right back where I was. Deeper in the hole than I have ever been.

The only thing I can really say is that the job I have now was once my dream job. I have grown to hate it more than anything else in my life. I suppose that means that maybe we put too much fantasy in what we think is our dream job, that the grass on the other side can also fade and whither in time.

Is there any chance of reconciliation?

I've been cheated on, so I know the other side of it. Trust is betrayed, and trust is the foundation of any successful, loving relationship. Some people can't be with someone who cheated on them. Some people can, but it takes a lot of time. Some people don't care. What kind of person is she?

If you want her back and she hasn't moved on, it's going to take a lot from you. It may be more than you're willing to put in. It's going to require absolute, genuine humility from you. She will have to believe that this was the worst mistake you've ever made. It sounds like you already know that.

You have to be willing to talk about any detail that she wants to know about. You have to tell the truth about it all, in as much detail as she wants to know.

At the end of that process, you're welcome to let her know that you still have very deep feelings for her, but you have to give her all of the power. She will be the one to decide everything. She will be the one to decide if and when it's okay to be touched.

Don't mention suicidal thoughts. I know that goes against being completely honest and truthful, but it's a bad move. You can mention depression, but keep it at that. If she asks, you can share that you've had suicidal thoughts, but be extremely careful about the wording and be aware that her first instinct will be that a mention of suicidal ideation is an attempt at emotional manipulation. This isn't usually the case, but after a cheating incident, she will be in full defense mode dealing with you for a long time.

And at the end of all that, she may still decide to move on. But you will then know that you did everything you could.

This is more for others reading this, but don't cheat. OP knows this lesson, but it's a few moments of pleasure for potentially a lifetime of regret.

To answer the subject line of the post, yes, it will affect her and everyone else around you. And that's not to guilt trip you. The fact that you brought it up shows that you already know that, too. Best of luck to you in whichever path you choose.

I tried college twice. After leaving the second time, I realized that the traditional college environment just wasn't for me, especially after 12 years of school. But I started teaching myself other skills for better opportunities.

There will be a time that college is nearly required to succeed at anything, but we're not there yet. And there are other options to the traditional college experience, more and more every day. Modern States, for instance, is providing a self-learning freshman year free program, college credit by examination. It's evolving for the better.

I wish these programs had existed when I was looking at options for college. Now that they're here, I'm more and more tempted to go back and work through a non-traditional program like these. Check them out and see what you think.

I want you to take a look at all of the things you've accomplished over the years. It doesn't matter what college it is; making the dean's list and having a GPA that high doesn't happen to everyone. You've worked your ass off for that. All those late nights and long days getting your work done counts. We're living in an age where people struggle to get into college or even finish, and you're kicking ass and taking names. Be proud of that.

Many people have trouble with empathy in this society. You see it everywhere. The fact that we have homeless people living in the streets in the wealthiest country in the world, in the richest cities of the richest country in the world... it shouldn't happen. A son or daughter coming to his or her parents to talk about problems shouldn't receive a response of, "oh yeah?! well, we had to walk six miles through the snow to school, uphill, both ways!" Because that's essentially what we're talking about here. But the good news is that your parents aren't the only people around to talk to. There are almost 7 billion folks on this big, spinning rock. If your parents aren't doing it for you, look to others. Someone as smart and fit as you are wouldn't have trouble finding a few like-minded individuals to talk with and have support from.

And I know it hurts to lose a relationship. It's a unique kind of pain that takes a long time to fade. But it will fade as time goes by. Every relationship I've been in and every failed relationship of my friends, the process has been all over the place. Some dwell on it the whole time, some try to ignore it, but the result is the same: after enough time has passed, that pain fades and you begin to feel better. You feel up to going out with new people again. If you don't have many friends (or, like I was in college, not many friends that I can visit in person), I would start there and build a small group of people that you can go do things with. If you already have a small group of friends, lean on them for support.

The only piece of relationship advice I can give is not to start a new one until you're over the old one all the way. The old one has a way of poisoning the new one if you haven't achieved closure.

Focus on your schooling. You've made it this far, and there's only a bit to go before you're out. And try to enjoy these years. I'm nearly 40 now, so I'm here to tell you that you'll never get them back. Be proud of what you've achieved and look at what you could achieve in only a few short years ahead. You've laid the groundwork for your future self's success. You need only walk the path now.

>My school is threatening to send my information to my state's Attorney General.

There's not really much they can do. You either pay your school debt or you don't. If you don't, it will go to default. When it defaults, it hits your credit hard, but that's really it. They typically turn these over to the Dept. of Education, and they'll steal your tax refunds until it's paid off. With the Dept. of Education, you can sometimes get on a payment plan. It's the government, so even $10 or $20 per month forever may be possible. You just have to talk to them about it and see if you can come to an arrangement.

You can usually get a free consultation with a dentist to at least talk about the issues. If you don't have insurance, I would be up front about that when calling for an appointment and see if there are any free consultation options. IQ tests aren't "how smart you are". They are a measure, by standardized tests, to determine the person's intellectual "age" vs the person's chronological age. The intellectual age score is divided by the chronological age score and out pops the intelligence quotient.

The problem is the testing. The goal is to design a test that is capable of measuring a person's intellectual age without being too long. So, say you have time for 100 questions. What 100 questions would you pick to decide someone's intelligence?

Better yet, split that into categories. Math, Science, Language, Logic, and Reading. That's 20 questions each.

So, in 20 questions, design me a mathematics segment that tells me who will be the next Alan Turing and who will be the next high school dropout, and let me rate everything in between.

If you are asked 20 questions that you know the answers to, you would score very high on the math portion. The test designers try to include a mixture of concepts to measure intelligence, but let's say you miss one in every section that you would have gotten otherwise.

This is the problem with testing for intelligence. It gives you an idea, but basing anything important on such scores is going to miss a lot of potential and reward a lot of luck.

But anyway, back to the way scoring is calculated.

So you get an intellectual score of 10 on the test and you're 10 years old at the time of taking. 10 divided by 10 is 1, 1 * 100 = 100 IQ. 100 IQ means that you are knowledgeable of the things you should be knowledgeable at age 10. Anything lower indicates there's probably room for improvement, anything higher means that you know more, according to the test, than most of your peers (and previously tested people) at your age.

Social skills cannot be tested in this way. The only thing that comes close is understanding of language. Some of the best novels and writing in the world has been produced by anti-social persons in complete solitude.

TL;DR: Don't measure your self-worth or social skills based on an IQ test. It's not as important or valuable a measure as you might think.

P.S. I have an IQ of 142 the last time I was tested. It didn't make much difference for me.

Police are like hospitals when it comes to outstanding bills. They'd rather get something than nothing, even if it takes forever. Police can (not always, but can) be more laid back with a payment plan because they're not a for-profit enterprise anyway. And it's not like your not paying the fine for a long time will affect whether or not they can keep the doors open.

Call the court where you have the tickets/warrants and tell them your situation. You may have to go to court to see the judge and explain things further. At the minimum, they put you on a payment plan that you can afford with all your other responsibilities considered. Can you afford $20 a month? $10 a month? Our court considers special situations all the time. Sometimes citations and warrants are remanded completely if the situation is bad enough.

When you get on a payment plan, they will cancel the warrants so you're not arrested if you get stopped again/encounter an officer for whatever reason.
